title: The prayer at forty
hook: at forty a person prays: inspire me to be grateful for Your favor on me and my parents (46:15)

segments.voice: Yesterday, jathiyah, and your line was each called to its book. What did you write on your page on purpose? Day five hundred seventy-six.

Forty is the birthday people joke about. Black balloons, over-the-hill cards, a friend who buys you reading glasses as a gag. Somewhere around then, a lot of people take stock: the career, the body, the parents getting older. Surah Al-Ahqaf, the Sand Dunes, the forty-sixth surah, also marks forty. But it doesn't hand you a joke or a crisis. It hands you a prayer, and the first thing that prayer asks for is gratitude.

Verse fifteen begins with parents. It says a mother carries her child with hardship and gives birth with hardship, and that the carrying and the weaning take thirty months. Then it follows that child all the way to full strength, to forty years, and puts words in their mouth. In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Arouse me that I may give thanks for the favour wherewith Thou hast favoured me and my parents." The Arabic for arouse me is awzi'ni. It's an unusual word. Commentators explain it as inspire me, or rouse me, or keep me constantly at it, as if gratitude were something you need help even to remember. Look at who's in the prayer. Not just me. Me and my parents. At forty, many people finally understand what their parents carried, sometimes because they're carrying it now. The prayer goes on: that I may do good that pleases You, make my children good for me, and I turn to You in repentance. Three generations in one breath. And here's a thread you may remember from earlier this year. When Sulayman heard the ant warning her colony, in Surah An-Naml, he smiled and prayed with the same opening: rabbi awzi'ni, my Lord, rouse me to thank You for Your favor on me and my parents. A king at the height of power and an ordinary person at forty reach for the same words. Commentators note why forty matters: the age of maturity in judgment, and the age at which, according to the biographies, revelation first came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
screen: `THIRTY MONTHS OF CARRYING AND WEANING.` · `AWZI'NI: ROUSE ME TO THANK YOU.` · `ME AND MY PARENTS, THEN MY CHILDREN.` · `SULAYMAN PRAYED THE SAME WORDS.`

segments.voice: The practice is to pray it for yourself, whatever your age. Sit, and breathe. Bring your parents to mind, or whoever raised you, as they are or as they were. Think of one thing they carried for you that you didn't see at the time. If you pray, you can say the opening of the verse quietly: my Lord, rouse me to thank You for Your favor on me and my parents. If you don't, simply hold that one thing they carried, and say thank you in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Rabbi awzi'ni: my Lord, rouse me to give thanks, for me and my parents, from 46:15. Today's word.
Your line: inspire me to thank. Today, thank a parent or the person who raised you for one specific thing, or, if they're gone, say it aloud for them. Day five hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Many Muslims memorize the prayer of 46:15 and say it in their own supplications, often especially around the age of forty, and many also say Sulayman's matching words from 27:19.

fork.setup: you reach forty, full strength. according to 46:15, what is the first thing the prayer asks for?
options: to be roused to give thanks.
fork.reveal: the prayer opens by asking to be inspired to gratitude, for favor on you and your parents.

original.note: Arabic: my Lord, rouse me (to give thanks); in 46:15 and 27:19.

trapdoor: what you thought: forty is a crisis age.
what it means: in 46:15, forty is when a person prays to be roused to gratitude for themselves and their parents.
what a scholar hears: awzi'ni is rare and explained as 'inspire me, keep me at it'; the same words come from Sulayman in 27:19.
